You are working in /workspace, which contains the "Flasky" social blogging Flask application (Miguel Grinberg's Flask Web Development, 2nd edition structure). The Python code, templates, config.py, flasky.py, setup.py and requirements.txt already exist. Do NOT modify or create any .py file, any file under app/, or requirements.txt / setup.py / config.py / flasky.py.

Your job is to create ONLY these six top-level boilerplate files, and nothing else:

1. /workspace/.gitignore — standard Python/Flask gitignore: __pycache__/, *.py[cod], *.egg-info/, build/, dist/, .eggs/, venv/, .venv/, env/, *.sqlite, data-dev.sqlite, data.sqlite, .coverage, htmlcov/, tmp/, .pytest_cache/, .idea/, .vscode/, .DS_Store, *.log, .env, .flaskenv (comment that one as optional), chromedriver, geckodriver.

2. /workspace/LICENSE — the full standard MIT License text, copyright line: "Copyright (c) 2017 Miguel Grinberg".

3. /workspace/Procfile — Heroku Procfile for this app. Two lines:
   web: gunicorn flasky:app
   release: flask deploy

4. /workspace/Dockerfile — a Dockerfile based on `python:3.6-alpine`. It should: create a non-root `flasky` user, set WORKDIR /home/flasky, copy requirements.txt, create a virtualenv at venv and pip install -r requirements.txt plus gunicorn, copy app/ migrations/ flasky.py config.py boot.sh, make boot.sh executable, set ENV FLASK_APP flasky.py and ENV FLASK_CONFIG docker, chown -R flasky:flasky ./, USER flasky, EXPOSE 5000, ENTRYPOINT ["./boot.sh"]. Follow the exact style of the official flasky Dockerfile.

5. /workspace/boot.sh — a POSIX shell script starting with `#!/bin/sh`, that activates the venv, then loops retrying `flask deploy` until it succeeds (sleeping 5s between attempts and echoing "Deploy command failed, retrying in 5 secs..."), then execs `gunicorn -b :5000 --access-logfile - --error-logfile - flasky:app`. Make it executable (chmod +x).

6. /workspace/docker-compose.yml — version "3" compose file with two services:
   - `flasky`: builds `.`, image name `flasky:latest`, ports "8000:5000", restart always, environment: FLASK_CONFIG=docker, SECRET_KEY, MAIL_USERNAME, MAIL_PASSWORD, DATABASE_URL=mysql+pymysql://flasky:flasky@mysql/flasky (read SECRET_KEY/MAIL_* from the host env with ${...} interpolation), depends_on mysql.
   - `mysql`: image mysql/mysql-server:5.7, restart always, environment MYSQL_RANDOM_ROOT_PASSWORD=yes, MYSQL_DATABASE=flasky, MYSQL_USER=flasky, MYSQL_PASSWORD=flasky.

Also create 7. /workspace/README.md — a thorough README for the project. It must include: a title and short description; a feature list covering user authentication (registration, email confirmation, password reset, email change, Gravatar avatars, remember-me), role-based permission control (User / Moderator / Administrator with the Permission bit flags FOLLOW=1, COMMENT=2, WRITE=4, MODERATE=8, ADMIN=16), blog posts with Markdown/rich text, comments with moderation, and a follower system; the project directory tree; installation instructions (`pip install -r requirements.txt` and `pip install -e .`); how to set up the database (`export FLASK_APP=flasky.py`, `flask db upgrade`, `flask deploy`); how to run (`flask run`); a "Python API" section showing the two canonical import lines:
    from flask import current_app
    from app.models import User, Role, Post, Comment, create_app, db, fake, AnonymousUser, Permission, Follow
   plus short runnable snippets for creating a user (`user.password = 'secret'`, `user.verify_password('secret')`), creating a Post, creating a Comment, and following a user (`user1.follow(user2)`, `user1.is_following(user2)`); a REST API section documenting every endpoint under the `/api/v1` prefix — GET /api/v1/users/<int:id>, GET /api/v1/users/<int:id>/posts/, GET /api/v1/users/<int:id>/timeline/, GET /api/v1/posts/, POST /api/v1/posts/, GET /api/v1/posts/<int:id>, PUT /api/v1/posts/<int:id>, GET /api/v1/comments/, GET /api/v1/comments/<int:id>, GET /api/v1/posts/<int:id>/comments/, POST /api/v1/posts/<int:id>/comments/, POST /api/v1/tokens/ — noting that all API requests need HTTP Basic auth (email+password, or token as username with empty password) and that the account must be confirmed; a note about the environment (Python 3.9, Flask 0.12.2); and a MIT license note. Use proper GitHub-flavored Markdown. Verify the endpoint list against the real code in /workspace/app/api/*.py before writing (read those files first).

Report back a one-line confirmation listing the files you created. Do not create any other files.

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Flasky Flasky is a social blogging application built with [Flask](http://flask.pocoo.org/). It is the companion application from Miguel Grinberg's *Flask Web Development, 2nd edition*, and it demonstrates a complete, production-shaped Flask project: an application factory with blueprints, database migrations, token based authentication, role based access control and a JSON REST API. Users can register and confirm their account by email, write Markdown-formatted blog posts, comment on the posts of others, moderate abusive comments and follow each other to build a personalized timeline. ## Features ### User authentication - Registration with a confirmation email; unconfirmed accounts are restricted until the emailed token is used. - Login and logout backed by [Flask-Login](https://flask-login.readthedocs.io/), including a **remember me** option that keeps the session alive across browser restarts. - Password change for logged-in users, and a **password reset** flow by email for users who are locked out. - **Email change** confirmed through a token sent to the new address. - Passwords are never stored: only a salted hash is kept, exposed through a write-only `password` property and a `verify_password()` method. - User profiles with a name, location, biography, member-since and last-seen timestamps, and **Gravatar** avatars derived from the MD5 hash of the email address. ### Role-based permission control Every user is assigned exactly one role, and every role is a bit field built from the `Permission` flags: | Flag | Value | Grants | | --- | --- | --- | | `Permission.FOLLOW` | `1` | Follow other users | | `Permission.COMMENT` | `2` | Comment on posts written by others | | `Permission.WRITE` | `4` | Write original blog posts | | `Permission.MODERATE` | `8` | Suppress offensive comments written by others | | `Permission.ADMIN` | `16` | Full administrative access | The three roles created by `Role.insert_roles()` are: | Role | Permissions | Value | | --- | --- | --- | | `User` | `FOLLOW`, `COMMENT`, `WRITE` | `7` (the default role) | | `Moderator` | `FOLLOW`, `COMMENT`, `WRITE`, `MODERATE` | `15` | | `Administrator` | `FOLLOW`, `COMMENT`, `WRITE`, `MODERATE`, `ADMIN` | `31` | Permissions are checked with `user.can(Permission.WRITE)` and `user.is_administrator()`, and enforced on views with the `@permission_required` / `@admin_required` decorators. The `AnonymousUser` class implements the same interface so that unauthenticated requests can be checked without a special case. ### Blog posts - Composed in **Markdown** with a client-side rich text preview (Flask-PageDown), rendered server-side with `markdown` and sanitized with `bleach` before being cached in the `body_html` column. - Permalinks for individual posts, pagination of the post list, and in-place editing restricted to the author or an administrator. - The home page can be toggled between *all posts* and *posts from the people you follow*. ### Comments with moderation - Any user with `Permission.COMMENT` can comment on a post; comments are also Markdown-rendered and sanitized. - Moderators (`Permission.MODERATE`) get a moderation queue where individual comments can be disabled and re-enabled; disabled comments stay hidden from regular users. ### Follower system - A self-referential many-to-many relationship implemented through an explicit `Follow` association model, so the follow timestamp is preserved. - `follow()`, `unfollow()`, `is_following()` and `is_followed_by()` helpers, followers/following listings, and a `followed_posts` join query that powers the timeline. - `User.add_self_follows()` makes every user follow themselves so their own posts appear in their timeline. ### Other niceties - Application factory (`create_app`) with per-environment configuration classes (`development`, `testing`, `production`, `heroku`, `docker`, `unix`). - Database migrations with Flask-Migrate/Alembic. - Fake user, post and comment generators (`app.fake`) for populating a development database. - Custom `flask` CLI commands: `deploy`, `test` (with optional coverage) and `profile`. - Deployment support for Heroku (`Procfile`) and Docker (`Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `boot.sh`). ## Project structure ``` . ├── app/ # application package │ ├── __init__.py # application factory, extension objects │ ├── decorators.py # permission_required / admin_required │ ├── email.py # asynchronous email support │ ├── exceptions.py # ValidationError │ ├── fake.py # fake data generators │ ├── models.py # Permission, Role, Follow, User, Post, Comment │ ├── api/ # REST API blueprint (/api/v1) │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── authentication.py # HTTP Basic auth + token endpoint │ │ ├── comments.py │ │ ├── decorators.py │ │ ├── errors.py │ │ ├── posts.py │ │ └── users.py │ ├── auth/ # authentication blueprint (/auth) │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── forms.py │ │ └── views.py │ ├── main/ # main blueprint (/) │ │ ├── __init__.py │ │ ├── errors.py │ │ ├── forms.py │ │ └── views.py │ ├── static/ │ │ ├── favicon.ico │ │ └── styles.css │ └── templates/ │ ├── auth/ # login, register, password/email flows │ ├── mail/ # notification emails │ ├── base.html │ ├── index.html │ ├── post.html │ ├── user.html │ └── ... ├── migrations/ # Alembic migration environment ├── config.py # configuration classes ├── flasky.py # application entry point and CLI commands ├── setup.py # packaging metadata ├── requirements.txt # pinned dependencies ├── boot.sh # Docker container entry point ├── Dockerfile ├── docker-compose.yml ├── Procfile # Heroku process types ├── LICENSE └── README.md ``` ## Installation Clone the repository, create and activate a virtual environment, then install the dependencies and the package itself: ```bash python -m venv venv source venv/bin/activate # on Windows: venv\Scripts\activate pip install -r requirements.txt pip install -e . ``` Installing with `pip install -e .` puts the `app` package on the Python path in editable mode, so changes to the source are picked up without reinstalling. ### Configuration Configuration is read from environment variables (see `config.py`). The most useful ones are: | Variable | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `FLASK_APP` | Must be `flasky.py` for the `flask` CLI to find the app | | `FLASK_CONFIG` | Configuration name: `development` (default), `testing`, `production`, `heroku`, `docker`, `unix` | | `SECRET_KEY` | Secret used to sign sessions and tokens | | `DATABASE_URL` | SQLAlchemy database URL (defaults to a local SQLite file) | | `MAIL_USERNAME`, `MAIL_PASSWORD` | Credentials for the outgoing mail server | | `FLASKY_ADMIN` | Email address that is granted the `Administrator` role on registration | These can also be placed in a `.env` file, which is loaded automatically. ## Setting up the database ```bash export FLASK_APP=flasky.py # on Windows: set FLASK_APP=flasky.py flask db upgrade # create/upgrade the database schema flask deploy # run all deployment tasks ``` `flask deploy` is idempotent and does three things: it upgrades the database to the latest migration, creates or updates the `User`, `Moderator` and `Administrator` roles, and makes sure every existing user follows themselves. Run it after every deployment and after pulling new migrations. To populate a development database with fake content: ```bash flask shell >>> from app import fake >>> fake.users(100) >>> fake.posts(100) >>> fake.comments(100) ``` ## Running the application ```bash export FLASK_APP=flasky.py flask run ``` The application is then available at . Other useful commands: ```bash flask test # run the unit tests flask test --coverage # run the tests under coverage flask profile # run the app under the code profiler flask shell # shell with db and the models pre-imported ``` ### Running with Docker ```bash export SECRET_KEY= export MAIL_USERNAME= export MAIL_PASSWORD= docker-compose up --build ``` This starts the application behind gunicorn on port 8000, together with a MySQL 5.7 container. `boot.sh` retries `flask deploy` until the database container is ready, then launches gunicorn. ### Deploying to Heroku The `Procfile` declares the two process types Heroku needs: ``` web: gunicorn flasky:app release: flask deploy ``` The `release` phase runs `flask deploy` on every deployment, so migrations and roles are always up to date. Set `FLASK_CONFIG=heroku` and `FLASK_APP=flasky.py` in the Heroku config vars. ## Python API All the models and the application factory are re-exported from `app.models`, so a script or shell session only needs two imports: ```python from flask import current_app from app.models import User, Role, Post, Comment, create_app, db, fake, AnonymousUser, Permission, Follow ``` Every snippet below assumes an active application context: ```python app = create_app('development') app.app_context().push() db.create_all() Role.insert_roles() ``` ### Creating a user The `password` attribute is write-only: assigning to it stores a hash, and the plaintext can only be checked with `verify_password()`. ```python user = User(email='john@example.com', username='john') user.password = 'secret' # hashed on assignment db.session.add(user) db.session.commit() user.verify_password('secret') # True user.verify_password('wrong') # False user.role.name # 'User' (the default role) user.can(Permission.WRITE) # True user.can(Permission.ADMIN) # False user.gravatar(size=256) # avatar URL token = user.generate_confirmation_token() user.confirm(token) # True, and sets user.confirmed ``` An anonymous visitor is represented by `AnonymousUser`, which answers the same questions negatively: ```python AnonymousUser().can(Permission.FOLLOW) # False AnonymousUser().is_administrator() # False ``` ### Creating a post Assigning to `body` triggers the Markdown renderer, which fills `body_html` with sanitized HTML. ```python post = Post(body='This is my **first** post!', author=user) db.session.add(post) db.session.commit() post.body_html # '

This is my first post!

' post.to_json() # dict ready to be returned by the API Post.from_json({'body': 'Written through the API'}) ``` Reading posts back, newest first, using the configured page size: ```python Post.query.order_by(Post.timestamp.desc()).paginate( 1, per_page=current_app.config['FLASKY_POSTS_PER_PAGE'], error_out=False).items ``` ### Creating a comment ```python comment = Comment(body='Nice post!', author=other_user, post=post) db.session.add(comment) db.session.commit() post.comments.count() # 1 comment.disabled = True # what a moderator does to hide a comment db.session.commit() ``` ### Following a user ```python user1 = User(email='user1@example.com', username='user1', password='cat') user2 = User(email='user2@example.com', username='user2', password='dog') db.session.add_all([user1, user2]) db.session.commit() user1.follow(user2) db.session.commit() user1.is_following(user2) # True user2.is_followed_by(user1) # True user1.followed.count() # 1 user2.followers.count() # 1 # posts written by the people user1 follows (the timeline) user1.followed_posts.order_by(Post.timestamp.desc()).all() user1.unfollow(user2) db.session.commit() user1.is_following(user2) # False ``` The follow relationship is stored in the `Follow` model, which keeps the timestamp of the association: ```python Follow.query.filter_by(follower=user1, followed=user2).first().timestamp ``` ## REST API The API blueprint is registered under the `/api/v1` prefix. ### Authentication **Every** API request must carry HTTP Basic credentials — there are no anonymous endpoints, including `POST /api/v1/tokens/`. Two forms are accepted: - **Email and password**: the Basic auth username is the account's email address and the password is the account password. - **Token**: the Basic auth username is an API token and the **password is left empty**. The account must also be **confirmed**; an authenticated but unconfirmed user receives `403 Forbidden` with `{"error": "forbidden", "message": "Unconfirmed account"}`. Failed authentication returns `401 Unauthorized` with `{"error": "unauthorized", "message": "Invalid credentials"}`. Tokens are obtained with email and password (a token cannot be used to mint another token) and expire after one hour. ### Endpoints | Method | Endpoint | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | `POST` | `/api/v1/tokens/` | Request an API token. Must be called with email and password; returns `{"token": ..., "expiration": 3600}`. | | `GET` | `/api/v1/users/` | Retrieve a single user. | | `GET` | `/api/v1/users//posts/` | Retrieve the posts written by a user, newest first (paginated). | | `GET` | `/api/v1/users//timeline/` | Retrieve the posts followed by a user, newest first (paginated). | | `GET` | `/api/v1/posts/` | Retrieve all the blog posts (paginated). | | `POST` | `/api/v1/posts/` | Create a blog post owned by the authenticated user. Requires `Permission.WRITE`. Returns `201` with a `Location` header. | | `GET` | `/api/v1/posts/` | Retrieve a single blog post. | | `PUT` | `/api/v1/posts/` | Update a blog post. Requires `Permission.WRITE`, and the caller must be the author or an administrator. | | `GET` | `/api/v1/comments/` | Retrieve all the comments, newest first (paginated). | | `GET` | `/api/v1/comments/` | Retrieve a single comment. | | `GET` | `/api/v1/posts//comments/` | Retrieve the comments on a post, oldest first (paginated). | | `POST` | `/api/v1/posts//comments/` | Add a comment to a post. Requires `Permission.COMMENT`. Returns `201` with a `Location` header. | Note that the collection endpoints end with a trailing slash, while the single-resource endpoints do not. ### Pagination Collection endpoints accept a `?page=` query string argument and return an envelope alongside the items: ```json { "posts": [ ... ], "prev": "/api/v1/posts/?page=1", "prev_url": "/api/v1/posts/?page=1", "next": "/api/v1/posts/?page=3", "next_url": "/api/v1/posts/?page=3", "count": 142 } ``` `prev`/`next` are `null` when there is no previous or next page, and `count` is the total number of items in the collection. Page sizes come from the `FLASKY_POSTS_PER_PAGE` and `FLASKY_COMMENTS_PER_PAGE` configuration values. Comment collections use the `comments` key instead of `posts`. ### Error responses Errors are returned as JSON with an `error` and a `message` key: | Status | `error` | | --- | --- | | `400` | `bad request` (also returned for a `ValidationError`, e.g. a post with no `body`) | | `401` | `unauthorized` | | `403` | `forbidden` | | `404` | `not found` | | `500` | `internal server error` | ### Examples Using [HTTPie](https://httpie.org/), which is included in `requirements.txt`: ```bash # request a token (email + password) http --auth john@example.com:secret POST http://localhost:5000/api/v1/tokens/ # use the token as the username, with an empty password http --auth : GET http://localhost:5000/api/v1/posts/ # write a post http --auth : POST http://localhost:5000/api/v1/posts/ \ body="Hello, *world*!" # comment on post 1 http --auth : POST http://localhost:5000/api/v1/posts/1/comments/ \ body="Great post!" # read someone's timeline http --auth : GET http://localhost:5000/api/v1/users/1/timeline/ ``` With `curl`: ```bash curl -u john@example.com:secret -X POST http://localhost:5000/api/v1/tokens/ curl -u : http://localhost:5000/api/v1/posts/ ``` ## Environment This project targets **Python 3.9** and pins **Flask 0.12.2**. All the other dependency versions are pinned in `requirements.txt`; install them with `pip install -r requirements.txt` to get a known-good environment. The Docker image is built on `python:3.6-alpine`. ## License This project is licensed under the MIT License — see the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for the full text. Copyright (c) 2017 Miguel Grinberg.
